posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
I was just wondering why the user of laser diodes with oval beams want to alter the beam to make it round? Rarely do any of us shoot to a square plates. 

I guess my question is, couldn't an oval pinhole be used with an oval beam in a spatial filter, thus allowing a more even coverage of a rectangular plate and cut down on the number of optics used in the set up, that is, the optics used to "round" the beam?

posts.author: geso
posts.content_md:
This is something I have wondered about also. I have an elliptical pinhole I have been meaning to try out. If you used an expended elliptical beam to 

cover a rectangular plate, it would have much less light loss, than a round beam being expanded to cover a rectangular plate.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: You would also need a way to allign the ellipse axis. If you have a jround beam and want to try an elliptical beam out then all you need is to insert a cylinderical lens. I have found round beams easier to deal with.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Yes, I agree. 

But for those with diodes and fabricating their own spatial filter a small "rotary stage" would accomplish the task. I put rotary stage in parenthesis as it does not have to be micrometer adjustable but simply a static slip ring made of nylon and able to be rotated manually. I would think the adjustment would not have to critical to the minute or second, but maybe just to the degree. So by hand would be an option. Other options might be even as simple as a double gear or worm gear.

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
An elliptical pinhole for spatially filtering an oval beam is not necessary. The focus will, hard to believe, be a circle, but after that it will diverge with the oval shape.

Hardly anyone shoots square plates, but almost everyone shoots off axis. An elliptical beam oriented properly, the widest part to the non-tilt axis, should give efficient coverage of the flux.

Using a cylinder lens to circularize the beam will add astigmatism, which could end up haunting you later downbeam.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: I often use to cylindrical lenses to make the beam colimated and round. I have not yet found a problem with astigmatism but I don't make HOEs either. A guess that is another reason to use anamorphic prisms.
